title: A growth rulebook that suppresses defects, twins, and disorder in arbitrary crystals

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a shared quantitative framework that predicts how to grow crystals with specified limits on defects across unrelated chemistries. Given material-specific inputs and controlled growth conditions, it would prescribe a protocol and predict the resulting crystal quality before growth. Its central task is to connect thermodynamic, kinetic and surface variables to the defects that actually appear, accurately enough to suppress relevant defects below stated functional thresholds.

Conceptual scope: dislocations, twins, disorder and mosaicity are related measures of crystal imperfection, but they are not interchangeable. Dislocations are line defects; twins involve differently oriented crystal domains related by a crystallographic operation; disorder concerns variation in atomic or molecular arrangements or occupancies; mosaicity describes variation in orientation among crystalline regions. A useful rulebook would address the relevant mechanisms and measurements for each material rather than reduce crystal quality to one universal score.

The word “arbitrary” identifies the long-term ambition, not a demonstrated capability or an assured endpoint. A convincing initial breakthrough would establish bounded transferability across several independently documented, defect-limited crystal classes. It would allow declared material-specific inputs and limited calibration while retaining a shared predictive framework. Literal absence of every defect is unnecessary; reliable suppression to functionally useful levels is the intended capability.

significance.text: If achieved, this framework would let researchers and manufacturers specify relevant crystal-quality requirements before growth and obtain a defensible prediction of whether a protocol will meet them. The direct advance would be reproducible control of bounded defect metrics in validated materials. It would replace some empirical optimization with prospective prediction, without implying unrestricted choice of every defect population.

The protein case supplies a concrete reason this could matter. The August 2025 review connects growth conditions to impurity incorporation, lattice defects and diffraction quality. In its account of growth outside pores, slower growth can reduce incorporated impurities and associated lattice defects, improving diffraction. Predictive control of such relationships could make structural measurements more reliable, although a successful intervention in proteins does not establish equivalent benefits in other crystal classes.

Conditional impact assessment: extending reliable defect suppression across inorganic crystals, organic semiconductors, quantum materials, framework solids and macromolecular crystals could improve devices and experiments where crystal quality is a demonstrated bottleneck. These are potential application domains, not evidence that defects dominate every member of those families. The proposed comparison with Bessemer processing expresses the possibility of an enabling materials advance. Comparable industrial scale, economics and societal impact would require separate demonstrations of throughput, yield, cost and useful performance.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is transferable predictive defect control, rather than the first quantitative explanation of crystal growth. The protein review already describes mechanistic models, experiments and useful interventions. The harder step is to turn such understanding into prospective predictions that remain accurate across materially different systems and cover the defect outcomes relevant to their intended use.

A concrete barrier is material dependence at the growth interface. The reviewed protein work describes requirements for pore shape and size that depend on the protein. Thus, even within macromolecular crystallization, a successful nucleating surface cannot simply be assumed to work for another target. A transferable framework would need to identify which material and surface properties govern an intervention, predict its useful range, and state when its assumptions fail.

Engineering synthesis: the framework must connect controllable growth conditions to measurable defect outcomes while keeping the desired crystal phase accessible. It must also distinguish improvement in nucleation, crystal size or diffraction quality from demonstrated suppression of a particular defect mechanism. Separate empirical recipes for each material would not establish the shared predictive capability, even if every recipe produced a better crystal.

Open scientific boundary: a single framework may not cover every solid or every defect mechanism. Stochastic incorporation may leave residual defects, and the attainable suppression may depend on the material and growth regime. The breakthrough therefore requires useful predictions with uncertainty and declared boundaries, rather than a promise of universally perfect crystals.

current_state.text: The August 2025 review by Nanev, Saridakis and Chayen describes protein crystal growth for diffraction as still relying substantially on trial and error after decades of research. It also reviews mechanistic progress and experiments in which porous materials improve nucleation, crystal size or diffraction quality for multiple proteins. Those achievements should accompany the account of persistent empirical practice: the field has useful mechanisms and interventions, but these examples do not demonstrate prospective control of dislocations, twins and disorder across unrelated crystal classes.

The supplied review reports that the protein article's identity was verified and that both its HTML and twelve-page PDF had complete, untruncated text extraction without reported extraction problems. Figure images were not inspected, so this record relies on the reviewed textual account rather than independent interpretation of figures. The supplied findings do not establish a numerical cross-class suppression benchmark, a common success rate or an independently replicated general protocol.

The earlier research attributes to a 2025 Chemical Reviews article an account of single-crystal battery electrodes in which grain boundaries and orientation affect performance. No source text for that article was available to the supplied evidence review, so the specific attribution remains unverified here. Even if confirmed, active work on electrode microstructure would establish the importance of crystal structure to performance; it would not by itself prove that a transferable suppression framework is absent.

The earlier research also attributes to the seventh crystal-structure-prediction blind test, reported in 2024, both a rare success involving disorder and a broader unresolved difficulty with disorder. The linked IUCr article had no captured source text available to the supplied review, so those details cannot be confirmed here. Predicting disorder in a structure and controlling its incorporation during growth are distinct achievements; evidence for one would not establish the other.

Evidence boundary: the original research invoked dislocation-free silicon and near-perfect industrial crystals as achieved precedents, but the supplied review did not substantiate their precise scope or the claimed transfer limits. They therefore cannot serve here as verified historical benchmarks. No cross-class rulebook is demonstrated in the material assessed by the supplied review. That is a bounded finding about this evidence, not proof of field-wide absence. The freshness record is empty, so the August 2025 protein review cannot establish the state of the entire field as of November 2026.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration, not an established standard: pre-register a test set containing a nitride or oxide independently documented as dislocation-limited, a small-molecule crystal with a documented twin or disorder problem, and a macromolecular crystal with a documented mosaicity problem. These are proposed eligibility requirements; the supplied evidence does not establish that particular materials already satisfy them. Silicon would be excluded as a deliberate choice to challenge transfer across the selected classes, without relying on the unverified industrial-silicon assertion.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed demonstration, not an established standard

completion_criteria.text: Before growth, the same quantitative framework should predict the protocols and relevant defect outcomes for every selected material. The demonstration should declare material-specific inputs, the calibration procedure and its limits, uncertainty estimates, and the predictions fixed before the decisive experiments. This makes the shared predictive mechanism testable. Searching growth conditions until a better crystal appears, or combining unrelated optimized recipes after the fact, would not meet this proposed criterion.
completion_criteria.label: Before growth, the same quantitative framework should predict

completion_criteria.text: Published protocols should produce the intended phase and meet pre-registered, functionally justified thresholds for the relevant defect, twin, disorder and mosaicity metrics. Verification should combine diffraction with appropriate real-space microscopy where informative and feasible; no single technique should be presumed to resolve every defect type in every material. Report sampling, measurement uncertainty, yield and failure rates so that a few unusually good crystals cannot stand in for reliable process performance.

completion_criteria.text: A second laboratory should reproduce the results using the disclosed framework and protocols, with any additional calibration reported. The demonstrated scope should state the tested materials, growth regimes, crystal dimensions and practical processing constraints. Success would establish transferability across that finite test set and support further prospective tests. It would not establish literal universality, unrestricted defect control or industrial scalability.

related_concepts.text: Roster-based distinction: CRX-07, “Predictive experimental selection of a chosen crystal form,” addresses which crystal form growth produces. CRX-13 addresses imperfections within the resulting crystalline material. Maintaining the target phase is a necessary constraint for CRX-13, but successful polymorph selection does not establish suppression of dislocations, twins or disorder. Conversely, a low-defect crystal need not be the desired form.

Roster-based distinction: CRX-03, “Chemical-accuracy prediction of which molecular crystal will form,” concerns prediction of the molecular crystal outcome. CRX-13 requires an experimentally actionable connection between growth conditions and defect populations. Better structure prediction could inform growth planning, but predicting a structure, including its disorder, does not by itself provide a protocol that controls the disorder during growth.

Roster-based overlap: CRX-11, “Diffraction-quality crystals of arbitrary macromolecules on demand,” shares the goal of obtaining useful macromolecular crystals. CRX-11 emphasizes access to crystals suitable for diffraction across macromolecular targets; CRX-13 emphasizes quantitative suppression of specified imperfections across different crystal classes. A protein nucleation intervention can contribute to either goal, but improved nucleation or diffraction alone does not establish a transferable defect-control rulebook.

Roster-based relationship: CRX-04, “Atomic ensembles measured from total X-ray scattering,” could help characterize structural variation, while CRX-12, “Continuous atomic-resolution crystallography inside working devices and static extreme environments,” could help examine crystals under conditions of use. These measurement objectives can help verify growth outcomes or their persistence in operation. Characterization supplies evidence about defects; predictive control of their formation remains a separate capability.

Roster-based relationship: CRX-05, “Experimental many-electron quantum states of real crystals,” may benefit from better-controlled crystalline samples, and CRX-10, “Laboratory sources that do facility-class coherent X-ray crystallography,” concerns measurement infrastructure that could support characterization. Neither is a substitute for a growth framework. Predicting or measuring the properties of a high-quality crystal remains an additional task beyond producing it.

change_log.change: Preserved CRX-13 and its title while explicitly bounding the ambition implied by “arbitrary crystals.”
change_log.reason: The concept remains meaningful, but demonstrations on a finite set would establish tested breadth rather than universal applicability.

change_log.change: Reframed the missing breakthrough as transferable predictive defect control and distinguished dislocations, twins, disorder and mosaicity.
change_log.reason: The reviewed protein literature already contains quantitative mechanisms; the innovation requires shared prediction of distinct defect outcomes rather than the first mechanistic link.

change_log.change: Integrated the protein review's mechanistic advances and successful porous-material interventions alongside persistent trial-and-error practice.
change_log.reason: An account limited to empirical practice would omit demonstrated progress and obscure the difference between partial interventions and the proposed cross-class capability.

change_log.change: Qualified the battery-electrode and blind-test assertions and retained them as unresolved source attributions.
change_log.reason: Neither source had captured text available to the supplied review. Missing evidence does not show that the assertions are false, but prevents presenting them as verified findings.

change_log.change: Removed reliance on industrial silicon as a verified benchmark while preserving the claim's uncertainty and the proposed exclusion of silicon from the test set.
change_log.reason: The supplied review did not substantiate the industrial achievement's precise scope or its transfer implications. The test-set choice can stand independently.

change_log.change: Bounded the revolutionary impact claim to prospective control of specified quality metrics and retained the Bessemer analogy as a conditional judgment.
change_log.reason: Suppression below thresholds does not establish arbitrary defect design, economic transformation or industrial scalability.

change_log.change: Strengthened completion criteria with a shared framework, prospective predictions, bounded calibration, uncertainty, yield, failure reporting and independent replication.
change_log.reason: Successful protocols alone could result from separate empirical optimizations and would not demonstrate transfer of predictive control.

change_log.change: Preserved the dated evidence boundary, complete text extraction and uninspected figures, and distinguished related roster entries.
change_log.reason: The final record must not imply independent document inspection, current field-wide coverage or equivalence between growth control, crystal-form selection and characterization.

unresolved_issues: Can a shared framework predict useful defect suppression across unrelated crystal classes with only bounded material-specific calibration?
Which specific nitride or oxide, small-molecule crystal and macromolecular crystal satisfy the proposed test-set requirements? Their eligibility needs independent documentation.
What functional thresholds, sampling plans and complementary measurements would establish reliable suppression for each selected defect mechanism?
The battery-electrode and seventh-blind-test attributions remain unverified because their source texts were unavailable to the supplied review.
The precise scope of the industrial-silicon and near-perfect industrial-crystal precedents remains unsubstantiated in the supplied evidence.
Field-wide progress after the August 2025 protein review, including whether a transferable framework exists as of November 2026, remains unassessed because the freshness record is empty.

Residual stochastic defects, industrial scale, throughput, cost and resulting device-performance benefits require separate investigation; meeting the proposed laboratory criteria would not resolve them.
